What is the test pyramid, and when would you deviate from it?

Many unit tests, fewer integration tests, and a few end-to-end tests, since cost and fragility rise as you go up. Deviate when the risk is elsewhere. A thin CRUD service has little logic but a lot of SQL and wiring, so more integration tests with a real database (a shape sometimes called the "testing diamond") find more bugs than many mock-heavy unit tests.
Unit test vs integration test: where's the boundary?

A unit test exercises a unit in isolation, in memory, and doesn't touch I/O. An integration test checks that components work together with real infrastructure: SQL actually runs, JSON actually serializes. A class using a mock repository can pass while the query itself is broken. You need both.
What's the difference between JUnit Platform, Jupiter and Vintage?

Platform launches tests and defines the TestEngine API that IDEs and build tools use. Jupiter is the modern API and its engine. Vintage is an engine for old JUnit 3 and 4 tests. Splitting them means a new framework can run on the same platform, and tools don't depend on test-writing APIs.
What changed in JUnit 6?

It's an evolution of the same Jupiter API rather than a rewrite. All modules now share one version number, the minimum is Java 17, and Vintage is deprecated. Existing Jupiter tests generally keep working after a dependency change. Check the release notes for removed deprecated APIs.
Output: in what order do these callbacks run, and what does n print?

See the LifeTest run in the Lifecycle section. beforeAll runs once; then, for each test, ctor, beforeEach, the test, afterEach; then afterAll once. beforeEach prints n=0 every time, as each test gets a new instance. With @TestInstance(PER_CLASS), one instance is shared, so n would keep growing.
Why does JUnit create a new instance per test method?

To isolate tests: state in instance fields can't leak from one test to another, so tests can run in any order. That's why fields in a test class don't need resetting. Static fields are shared, so avoid mutable statics. A static counter in the constructor counted 24 instances in a run of 25 tests, showing that each test and each parameterized invocation gets its own.
@BeforeEach vs @BeforeAll? Why must @BeforeAll be static?

@BeforeEach runs before each test, on that test's instance. @BeforeAll runs once for the class, before any instance exists, so it has to be static. Under PER_CLASS, an instance exists first, so it needn't be. Use @BeforeAll for expensive shared setup, such as starting a server.
assertThrows vs assertThrowsExactly vs the JUnit 4 expected attribute?

assertThrows passes for the type or any subclass, and returns the exception. assertThrowsExactly needs the exact type: assertThrowsExactly(RuntimeException.class, ...) fails if an IllegalStateException is thrown, as a test run confirmed. JUnit 4's expected covered the whole method, so an exception from the setup lines could pass the test by mistake.
What's the difference between assertAll and consecutive assertions?

Normal assertions stop at the first failure. assertAll runs every one, and reports them together as a MultipleFailuresError. In a run, two failing assertions reported getFailures().size() == 2. It's handy when checking several properties of one result.
Assertion vs assumption?

A failed assertion means the test failed. A failed assumption aborts the test, which shows as skipped: a run displayed Assumption failed: skip. Use assumptions for environment preconditions that don't reflect a bug, such as a required external tool. Too many skipped tests hide problems, so use conditions and tags with care.
How would you test a method with many input combinations?

Use @ParameterizedTest with @CsvSource for readable tables, or @MethodSource for complex objects. Include boundary values, null, empty, and invalid inputs. Use @NullAndEmptySource for strings. Give a name so reports show which case failed. For properties that should hold for all inputs, jqwik offers property-based tests.

Mock vs stub vs spy vs fake?

A stub returns canned data. A mock also verifies interactions. A spy wraps a real object and can override parts. A fake is a light working implementation, such as an in-memory repository. Stubs support state verification (checking the result) and mocks support behaviour verification (checking the call). State verification breaks less on refactoring.
What do Mockito mocks return for unstubbed methods?

Defaults: 0 for numbers, false for boolean, null for objects, and empty for collections, Optional and Stream. Arrays return null. That's the behaviour of RETURNS_DEFAULTS. So a forgotten stub can give an NPE far from the mock, in the code under test.

Why does when(spy.get(0)) throw on an empty list? How do you fix it?

Java evaluates the argument of when() first, which calls the real get(0) on the real list, throwing IndexOutOfBoundsException. Use doReturn("a").when(spy).get(0), where when(spy) returns a stubbing proxy, and .get(0) on that isn't real. The same form is used for void methods.
What's the error here? when(t.f(anyInt(), "x")).thenReturn("y");

It throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException. Matchers register state on a stack, and Mockito needs one matcher per argument. Mixing a raw value breaks the count. Use eq("x"). A related error is using a matcher outside when or verify.
any() vs any(String.class)?
any() matches anything, including null. any(String.class) does a type check, and doesn't match null, since Mockito 2. So if the code passes null, the second doesn't match, and the stub isn't applied.
How does @InjectMocks decide how to inject? What are the pitfalls?

It tries the biggest constructor, then setters, then fields, in that order. It stays silent if it can't resolve something. Two mocks of the same type are matched by field name. Since constructor injection is used if possible, adding a new dependency passes null to it, so you get an NPE, not a compile error. Direct new in a setup method is more honest.
What are strict stubs? What is UnnecessaryStubbingException?

Strictness makes Mockito fail tests that have unused stubs (UnnecessaryStubbingException), and report argument mismatches from production code (PotentialStubbingProblem). It's the default with MockitoExtension. It's useful because stale stubs mislead readers. Common cause: shared stubs in @BeforeEach that only some tests use. Fix by moving them, or marking as lenient() if they're truly shared.
How do you test code using LocalDateTime.now() or UUID.randomUUID()?

Best: inject the dependency. Pass a java.time.Clock and use LocalDateTime.now(clock), with Clock.fixed(...) in tests. For IDs, inject a Supplier<UUID>. mockStatic is available for legacy code, but mocking java.time classes is fragile, and core JDK types can break, as the stack overflow with ArrayList showed.
How does Mockito mock final classes and static methods?

The default mock maker before version 5 created subclasses, so it couldn't override final members. The inline mock maker, default since Mockito 5, uses the instrumentation API to rewrite class bytecode, adding interception into the real class, with a per-thread check for active mocks. That's why static mocks are scoped to one thread.
How would you verify an object created inside the method under test?

Use ArgumentCaptor at the mock that receives it, then assert on its fields. If there's no collaborator to capture from, either the behaviour is visible in the return value, which you should test, or the class should get a factory.
How would you test a private method?

You normally don't. Test it through the public method that uses it. If it's complex enough to need its own tests, that's a sign it belongs in its own class with a public API. Reflection tests couple you to implementation details and block refactoring.
How do you test a method that runs asynchronously?

Split the logic into a synchronous method and test that directly. To test the async path, use CompletableFuture.get(timeout), or Awaitility for polling: await().atMost(5, SECONDS).until(...). Never use fixed Thread.sleep, which causes slow and flaky tests. For an @Async method in Spring, a synchronous TaskExecutor in the test config helps too.
What is a flaky test? What causes them, and what do you do about them?

A test that passes and fails with no code change. Causes: time and timing (sleep, midnight, time zones), shared state or data between tests, reliance on order (HashMap iteration), external services, and concurrency. Treat it as a bug. Quarantine it so the main build stays trustworthy, reproduce by running it repeatedly, then fix the cause. Don't just add retries, which train people to ignore failures.
@WebMvcTest vs @SpringBootTest with MockMvc?

@WebMvcTest loads only the web layer, so services must be replaced with @MockitoBean. It starts quickly and tests HTTP concerns. @SpringBootTest plus @AutoConfigureMockMvc loads everything, running through real services to the database: slower, higher confidence. A typical split is mostly slices, with a few full-flow tests.
@Mock vs @MockitoBean (and the old @MockBean)?

@Mock creates a Mockito mock without Spring, for plain unit tests. @MockitoBean puts a mock into the Spring context, replacing the bean of that type. It came with Spring Framework 6.2, and @MockBean was deprecated in Boot 3.4 and removed in Boot 4. Changing the set of mock beans creates a new cached context, so many varied combinations slow the suite.
Why does my @WebMvcTest fail with "No qualifying bean of type UserService"?

The slice doesn't scan @Service beans, so the controller's dependency is missing. Add @MockitoBean UserService. If @SpringBootApplication has extra annotations such as @EnableJpaAuditing, these apply to slices too, and can fail for the same reason. Move them to a separate @Configuration class.
Why might a repository test pass with H2 and fail in production?

Differences in SQL dialect, native queries, JSON and array types, case sensitivity, index and locking behaviour, and migrations written for PostgreSQL or MySQL. Also, Hibernate may generate H2 schema with ddl-auto while production uses Flyway. Use Testcontainers with the same database version and run your real migrations.
In @DataJpaTest, why call flush() and clear()?

Within one transaction, persist may not issue SQL yet, and a read may be served from the persistence context. So constraints wouldn't fire and mappings wouldn't be exercised. flush() sends the SQL, clear() empties the cache, and the following read really hits the database. Since the test rolls back, nothing persists.
Is it a good idea to put @Transactional on tests?

It gives automatic cleanup, but changes what you test. The test's transaction wraps the service's, so REQUIRES_NEW, commit-time constraints, @TransactionalEventListener and lazy-loading failures behave differently. With a real HTTP port, it doesn't roll back the server's work at all. Many teams prefer no test transaction for integration tests, and clean the tables with @Sql or truncation.
How does Spring's test context cache work, and how do you speed up a slow test suite?

The cache key combines configuration classes, profiles, properties, and mock definitions. Identical configurations reuse one context. To speed up: use slices, a shared base class, avoid @DirtiesContext, reduce varied @MockitoBean sets, share containers, and run in parallel where safe (Surefire forks or JUnit parallel execution). Also separate unit tests from integration tests so that feedback comes first.
What's the difference between Surefire and Failsafe?

Surefire runs unit tests in the test phase, matching names like *Test. Failsafe runs integration tests, named *IT, in the integration-test phase, and reports failure in verify, so that post-integration-test cleanup still runs. Run with mvn verify.
What does Testcontainers do, and how do you keep it fast?

It runs real services in Docker for your test's duration, through the Docker API. To keep it fast, use one static container shared by all classes, so startup happens once. Use small images and a pinned version. Clean data between tests instead of restarting the container. Combine with @ServiceConnection to avoid wiring properties by hand.
Is 100% coverage a good goal?

No. It rewards tests of trivial code, and coverage doesn't show that behaviour was checked: a test with no assertions counts. Aim for strong coverage on business logic and branches, and use it to find gaps. A sensible team uses a threshold on new code, reviews test quality, and uses mutation testing on critical parts. Branch coverage says more than line coverage.
Is TDD always worthwhile?

It works well for domain logic, algorithms and bug fixes, where a failing test proves the bug first. It's less suited to exploratory prototypes and UI, or integration with an unknown API, where you learn first and then write tests. A balanced answer describes when you'd use it, not an absolute position.
Scenario: A test passes alone but fails when the whole suite runs. How do you debug it?

It's a test isolation problem. Suspect shared mutable state: static fields, a singleton, database rows left by another test, a cached Spring context altered by a @MockitoBean or a modified bean, or system properties. Bisect: run with the class before it to find the polluter. Check that data is cleaned up. ThreadLocal left set, such as SecurityContextHolder, is also a common cause.
Scenario: You've inherited a legacy class with no tests and static calls. How do you start?

- Write characterization tests that pin current behaviour at the highest usable level.
- Find a seam: extract a method or wrap static calls behind an interface.
- Use mockStatic as a temporary measure.
- Refactor in small steps, then replace with focused unit tests.
The aim is to make change safe rather than to reach a number.
Scenario: How would you test a Kafka consumer that writes to a database?

Unit-test the handler's logic with plain objects. Use @SpringBootTest with Testcontainers for Kafka and the database for one realistic flow: publish, then use Awaitility to wait for the row. Cover duplicate delivery (idempotency), poison messages going to the dead-letter topic, and retries. @EmbeddedKafka is a lighter alternative, though it's not the same as a real broker.
How do you test a service that calls a third-party REST API?

Unit-test the business logic with the client interface mocked. Then test the client itself against a WireMock server (or MockRestServiceServer): stub realistic JSON, assert the mapping, verify the request (path, headers, body), and simulate 4xx/5xx, slow responses and connection resets to prove timeouts, retries and error translation. Point the base URL at WireMock with @DynamicPropertySource. Never call the real third-party API in automated tests.
What is ArchUnit and why would you use it?

A library that turns architecture rules into JUnit tests by inspecting bytecode: layer dependencies, no cycles between packages, naming conventions (*Controller only in web), no field injection, domain free of framework imports. It makes code review rules enforceable in CI, which matters most in large or hexagonal codebases.
Your tests have 40 lines of setup each and break whenever a constructor changes. How do you fix that?

Introduce test data builders (or an Object Mother) with valid defaults, so tests set only the fields relevant to the scenario and constructor changes are fixed in one place. Move shared Spring context setup into a common base or @TestConfiguration without breaking context caching, and check whether the class under test simply has too many dependencies, which is a design smell the tests are exposing.
Should a unit test have only one assertion?

The real rule is one behaviour per test. Checking several fields of one result is fine; use assertAll or AssertJ SoftAssertions so you see every failure at once. What to avoid is a test that exercises several scenarios in sequence, because the first failure hides the rest and the name can't describe what broke.

JUnit assertions vs AssertJ vs Hamcrest?

| JUnit Assertions | AssertJ | Hamcrest
Style | assertEquals(expected, actual) | assertThat(actual).isEqualTo(expected) | assertThat(actual, is(expected))
Discoverability | Small, fixed set | IDE autocomplete after the dot, per type | You must know the matcher names
Collections | Basic | containsExactly, extracting, filteredOn | hasItem, contains
Several checks at once | assertAll | SoftAssertions | None built in
Classic mistake | Swapping expected and actual | Forgetting the assertion method, e.g. assertThat(x); | Mixing up matcher imports
Rule of thumb: AssertJ for readable, type-aware assertions and clear failure messages; all three come with spring-boot-starter-test, so the choice is about team style.
@ValueSource vs @CsvSource vs @MethodSource vs @EnumSource?
MockMvc vs TestRestTemplate vs WebTestClient for controller tests?

| MockMvc | TestRestTemplate | WebTestClient
Real HTTP server | No, mock servlet environment | Yes, with webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT | Yes against a running server, or bound to MockMvc via MockMvcWebTestClient
Same thread as the test | Yes | No | Depends on the mode
@Transactional test rollback covers the request | Yes | No: the server commits in its own transaction | Only in mock mode
Works with @WebMvcTest | Yes | No | Yes, when bound to MockMvc
Style | Builder with andExpect | Classic RestTemplate calls | Fluent, also for WebFlux
Interview tip: with a real server, test data written by the request is not rolled back, so clean up explicitly (or start a fresh Testcontainers database) to keep tests independent.
